title: Playing with older men; joining Local 802
summary: He learned from older veterans, credits Cecil Smith, and joins the new Local 802 in 1922 for two dollars.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Well, he finally got a boy but I was out of high school when he was born. I was playing with older men. Well, it so happened that -- I say, I was always with older men, older men. And I learned a lot from them because they had experiences over there in France and everything. I used to listen. I couldn't say anything, but I'd listen. I used to hear a lot of things. And it was an education to me in a way, because I knew how to conduct myself from their experiences.

And I always was thankful that I met a fellow like Cecil Smith. And he and I were friends to the end. There was a white local called 310 in New York City. He belonged to it, he and Casco Williams. There was just about a dozen colored fellows in the local. But then, in 1922, a new local opened up, Local 902. And they took everybody in.
Cecil told me, -- because we were working with Honey

Potter at the time, Cecil told me, -- and the trombone player, Clinton Green, to meet him the next day and he'd take us down, because he had joined. He took us down there and we joined. Two dollars to join 802. Now it costs you $75. Two dollars and they put a little sheet in front of you and say, play that. That was nothing.

And, of course, when I joined Fletcher I was with the union. We were all union men, and Fletcher and Duke and all like that. 802 right straight through. I was just going to say how good those fellows were to me, those older men. And all through my career, I was always with older men. Now, I'm on myself now, because all of them are gone.
